title: The Birth at Shivneri
shortDescription: Shivaji, the boy who would build Swarajya, is born on a fortified hill above Junnar — the beginning of one of the Deccan's most consequential lives.
description: By tradition, on 19 February 1630, a son was born to Jijabai and Shahaji Bhonsle within the walls of Shivneri, the fort that commands the town of Junnar in the hill country of the Western Ghats. The child was named Shivaji, after the auspicious Kshatriya deity Shiva. His father, Shahaji, was a Maratha warlord serving the Nizamshahi Sultanate of Ahmadnagar and then the Adilshahi Sultanate of Bijapur. His mother, Jijabai, was a daughter of the Jadhav clan, and her influence — and her telling of the tales of Hindu lands and heroes — is given a shaping role in the young prince's formation by the chronicles. Junnar, where the family held lands, lay in a countryside of forts, passes and valleys that would define his entire life.
significance: The place and family of Shivaji's birth foreshadowed his whole career: a hill fortress, a Maratha service nobility, and a mother whose memory and bloodlines were counted as central to his inspiration. Shivaji's life went on to reshape the political map of the Deccan and laid the foundations of the Maratha state — whether the 1630 birth date itself is exact is a matter on which sources differ.

people.name: Shivaji (later Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj)
people.role: The child — future founder of Swarajya
people.note: Born at Shivneri by tradition in February 1630.

people.name: Jijabai
people.note: Daughter of the Jadhav clan; the chronicles credit her with forming her son's ideals.

people.name: Shahaji Bhonsle

title: The First Forts and the Rise of Swarajya
shortDescription: A young prince with a handful of hill-country companions begins to draw the neighbouring forts and valleys of the Sahyadri under one banner — the first step of Swarajya, self-rule.
description: Raised in the fortress world of the ghats and trained in arms and letters, Shivaji in his mid-teens began gathering the mavals — the martial hill people of the valleys around Pune — around the idea of a kingdom of his own. The chronicles record that he rode with companions of his own age, among them Yesaji Kank and Tanaji Malusare, and set about winning over the garrisons and lords of the hill forts one by one. This was not sudden conquest but a slow, shrewd building of alliances: oaths, gifts, marriage ties, and the careful placement of trusted men in local commands. The aim was homeland rule — Swarajya — wrested from the sultanates that parceled out the Deccan among their nobles.
significance: This phase explains everything that followed. Shivaji's power was never a massed imperial army to begin with; it was a network of hill forts and valley loyalties, held by men who knew every pass and stream. The movement from a warlord's concept to a lived polity begins here — and the meaning of 'Swarajya' itself, as both a political ideal and a demand for home rule, would echo far beyond his lifetime. (Early details rest largely on the Marathi chronicles and are treated by modern historians with care.)

title: Torna and the Beginning of Expansion
shortDescription: The young Shivaji seizes the strong hill fort of Torna — capturing the treasury and the walls that would anchor a new power.
description: Torna, a major hill fort of the Bijapur-controlled Deccan, was taken by Shivaji in or around 1646, according to the standard accounts. The fort was approached not by costly assault but through persuasion and surprise — its garrison won over or overwhelmed with the support of the surrounding hill country. A considerable treasure found within, recorded in the chronicles, was used to strengthen the foundations of the expanding movement, and the fort's name was renewed as Prachandgad — 'the mighty fort'. It became a keystone holding in the chain of strongholds that guarded the new territory.
significance: Torna is usually taken as the first decisive step of Shivaji's independent military expansion. It demonstrated a formula he would repeat: take the high ground quietly, secure the local population's loyalty, convert captured resources into further fortification — and let each summit command the valleys below.

people.name: Shivaji
people.role: Leader of the taking of Torna
people.note: Approximately eighteen when Torna was taken.

people.name: Yesaji Kank
people.note: Among the maval companions present in the early captures.

title: Rajgad — Building a New Power
shortDescription: The towering plateau-fort of Rajgad becomes the seat of an emerging kingdom — the workshop where Swarajya was founded.
description: From about 1648–49, Rajgad — the great ring-fort crowning the Sahyadri above the Maval valleys — became Shivaji's principal residence and stronghold. It was fortified and developed into a capital of the growing state: storerooms, workshops, reservoirs, gates and dwellings rose within its sheltering cliffs, and the court that governed the expanding Swarajya functioned from this mountain fastness for over two decades. Rajgad was not merely a refuge; it was the visible centre of an alternative political order taking shape in the ghats, protected by nature and by the loyalty of the surrounding country.
significance: A state needs more than soldiers — it needs a centre, administration, and a symbol. Rajgad played all three roles while the movement grew from a handful of forts into a polity with revenue, law and diplomacy. Its architecture, still traceable today, shows the scale of building works that contemporaries and later rulers found remarkable.

people.name: Shivaji
people.note: Made the fort his headquarters for the building of the state.

people.name: Moropant Trimbak Pingle
people.note: Served as a chief minister-like figure in the court that formed around the new power.

title: The Capture and Consolidation of Forts
shortDescription: Fort after fort — Kondhana, Purandar and others — passes into the possession of the rising power, consolidating a chain of defence across the ghats.
description: Across the late 1640s and early 1650s, the movement's grip on the hill country tightened. Forts such as Kondhana (later Sinhagad) and Purandar were captured and consolidated through a combination of surprise, persuasion, and the disciplined use of local knowledge. Each stronghold was repaired, provisioned and placed under trusted commanders — a decentralised system in which local captains held their posts in the ruler's name. The sultans of Bijapur, committed to campaigns elsewhere and slow to respond, watched territory slip from their grasp one summit at a time.
significance: Consolidation — not an easy speed of conquest but the secure holding of what was taken — was Shivaji's most distinctive quality as a military builder. A fortress network of this kind could not easily be retaken, which is why the Swarajya survived the repeated expeditions sent against it in the 1650s and 1660s. (The exact roster and dates of each fort's capture are reconstructed from chronicles and administrative records, with some variation between sources.)

people.name: Shivaji
people.note: Directing the capture and governance of the fort chain.

people.name: Tanaji Malusare
people.note: Celebrated in later tradition for the taking of Kondhana (Sinhagad).

title: Afzal Khan and the Battle of Pratapgad
shortDescription: A general sent by Bijapur to destroy the new power is met at a hill-fort in a confrontation that decided the fate of the young Swarajya.
description: By autumn 1659 the Adilshahi Sultanate of Bijapur had had enough. Afzal Khan, an experienced general, was dispatched with a large force to crush the movement and its leader. He pitched camp in the valleys below Pratapgad, an advanced fort in the hills above the Konkan. Negotiations were attempted; the two leaders agreed to meet. What happened at the meeting — the meeting itself, the encounter, and the death of Afzal Khan — is one of the most contested and retold episodes of the period; the Marathi chronicles describe Afzal Khan attempting treachery that turned against him. Whatever the precise sequence, on 10 November 1659 the confrontation ended with Afzal Khan dead, his army set upon from the fort and the passes, and a decisive victory for Shivaji's forces before Bijapur's generals could regroup.
significance: Pratapgad transformed the standing of Swarajya. The removal of Bijapur's most feared general, in the field, sent notice through the Deccan that the hill-state could not be dismissed. The battle also let the movement push toward the Konkan coast, bringing ports, revenues and a wider stage into reach. The day is remembered as a turning point in the rise of the Maratha power.

people.name: Shivaji
people.note: Present at the decisive meeting on the fort.

people.name: Afzal Khan

people.name: Siddi Hilal (Jawhar Khan)

title: The Siege of Panhala and the Escape
shortDescription: Besieged inside a fortress by a Bijapur army, the leader of Swarajya escapes through the rain and the ghats in one of the great flight-and-pursuit dramas of the age.
description: After Pratapgad, the war did not stop. In 1660 Bijapur mounted a fresh expedition. Siddi Jauhar's army closed in on Panhala, a commanding fort on the Kolhapur plateau where Shivaji had taken position, and blockaded it through the monsoon months. Food ran low and the siege pressed hard. In the darkness of a July night, in torrential rain, Shivaji slipped out of the fort with a small party on a route known to the hill people, bound for Vishalgad. The escape — with a Bijapur column in pursuit and a wide valley to cross before safety — culminated in the skirmish at Ghod Khind, remembered as Pavankhind.
significance: The Panhala episode shows both the desperation and the discipline of the movement at its lowest hour: a ruler willing to gamble his life on a night march, and captains willing to die holding the pass behind him. Its outcome — the party's survival and the fort of Vishalgad's eventual relief — kept the Swarajya alive through the most dangerous months of its early years.

people.name: Shivaji
people.note: Escaped Panhala by night on 13 July 1660 (traditional date).

people.name: Siddi Jauhar

people.name: Baji Prabhu Deshpande
people.note: Fell at Ghod Khind holding the pass behind the escaping party.

title: The Battle of Pavankhind
shortDescription: A handful of men hold a narrow defile against a pursuing army so that the rest can reach safety — a stand that passed into the affection and memory of the Marathas.
description: The pursuit of Shivaji's night escape from Panhala came to a head in the defile of Ghod Khind, a narrowing of the mountain route toward Vishalgad. There, according to the chronicles, the rearguard under Baji Prabhu Deshpande and his brother Fulaji turned and held the pass against the pursuing Bijapur force for hours — enough time for the escaped party to reach the fortress of Vishalgad and safety. Baji Prabhu himself fell in the pass, and the day became one of the most fiercely remembered in the movement's early history. The name Pavankhind — 'the defile of the wind' — is how the fight is traditionally remembered. (The exact numbers, timing and details rest on the chronicles; modern historians accept the general outline with care.)
significance: The rearguard's stand at Ghod Khind secured the survival of the movement's leader and the continuity of Swarajya at a moment of extreme peril. In Maratha tradition the episode became a founding story of loyalty and sacrifice — the model of the devoted commander dying for his sworn lord and the cause.

people.name: Baji Prabhu Deshpande

title: The Surat Campaign, 1664
district: Surat (then the Mughal port of Surat)
shortDescription: A raid on the richest port of the Indian Ocean world shakes the Mughal empire's commercial heart and announces a new power to the sea routes.
description: In January 1664, with the Mughal governor of the Deccan pressing on his country, Shivaji led a force to the coast and attacked Surat — the great commercial port of western India, whose wharves, factories and warehouses served traders from across the Indian Ocean and Europe. The town was entered and its wealth systematically taken; the European factories, including those of the English East India Company, were among those looted while the Company's servants sought safety in their compound and ships. The treasury and goods carried off were enormous, and the blow to Mughal prestige and to Surat's trade was immediate and stunning. The raid was a strategic act: strike at the source from which the Mughal war-effort and rival powers drew their wealth.
significance: Surat announced Shivaji to the wider world in a single stroke. European letters, Mughal correspondence and Persian chronicles alike record the fall of the port — the event placed Swarajya on the map of Indian Ocean politics and made the Mughal court take the Deccan's new power fully seriously. For the merchants and artisans of Surat, the raid was a catastrophe whose memory shaped how the city viewed the Marathas for a generation.

people.name: Shivaji
people.note: Directed the campaign personally.

people.name: Navab of Surat
people.note: Said (in the accounts) to have kept within the fortified area during the raid.

title: The Agra Episode and the Escape, 1666
district: Agra (then the Mughal capital, today in Uttar Pradesh)
shortDescription: Invited to the Mughal court, the Deccan's leader is made a pawn of imperial ceremony — and escapes from the capital of his would-be captors.
description: After years of intermittent warfare, the Mughal governorship, in the person of Mirza Raja Jai Singh, forced Shivaji toward a negotiated submission. In the peace that followed (the 1665 treaty of Purandar), Shivaji agreed to attend the court of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb at Agra. His reception in May 1666 proved insulting and menacing: given a place far below his expectations, and placed under guarded residence while his fate was debated. The chronicles recount a dramatic flight — an escape in disguise from the imperial capital — followed by a journey across India and a safe return to the Konkan by months' end. (European factory records and the chronicles agree on the broad shape — a period of detention and a famous escape — while the details differ between accounts.)
significance: The Agra episode is a hinge of Shivaji's career. It marked the limits of his conventional diplomacy against the Mughal empire, and the escape restored the movement at the very moment imperial coercion was about to close around it. The audacity of the escape became part of his legend and gave Swarajya a second wind — within years he was again taking forts and receiving momentum, having slipped the strongest empire in the subcontinent like water through a fist.

people.name: Shivaji
people.note: Detained at Agra from May 1666 and escaped before the year's end.

people.name: Aurangzeb
people.note: Reigning at Agra; his treatment of Shivaji's reception shaped the crisis.

people.name: Mirza Raja Jai Singh

title: The Return to Expansion and Recovery of Forts
location: Back in the Konkan and the forts
shortDescription: Returned from Agra, the movement resumes its advance — recovering forts, opening the Konkan, and pushing into the southern Deccan — toward the threshold of kingship.
description: The years after the Agra escape saw Swarajya expand on every front. Forts ceded or lost under the pressure of the mid-1660s were recovered, new strongholds were raised (including the construction and fortification of Raigad as a lasting capital), and the movement reached the sea and into the southern Maratha country. Korwon (Kolhapur's) Konkan ports and inland towns passed under Swarajya administration or tribute. Campaigns pressed toward the Karnataka borders with the co-operation of Shivaji's half-brother Ekoji's Karnataka holdings and against imperial outposts. By the early 1670s the territories under his rule or protection formed a continuous state from the hill country to the coast, rich in ports, passes and fortresses.
significance: This second expansion transformed a hill-refuge into a maritime state and set the stage for the coronation of 1674. It also made clear that imperial submission at Purandar and Agra had been tactical, not final: Swarajya's central proposition — legitimate, enduring self-rule in the Maratha country — was being consolidated before the entire region.

people.name: Shivaji
people.note: Directed recovery and coastal expansion after 1666.

people.name: Ekoji (Vyasraya) Bhonsle
people.note: Ruled the Karnataka possessions; relations between the brothers shaped the southern campaigns.

title: The Coronation at Raigad
shortDescription: On a monsoon-drenched summit, the ruler of Swarajya is crowned Chhatrapati — Shiva Chattrapati — in ceremonies that made his state an open claim to sovereignty.
description: On 6 June 1674, at his capital of Raigad, Shivaji was crowned with full sovereign rites. The coronation was delayed by disputes over the ritual lineage appropriate to a Maratha ruler (he had previously arranged de facto rule without the full ceremony), and priests were brought from far to satisfy the requirements of the Kshatriya consecration as then understood. The ceremony featured the golden umbrellas, seals, titles and processions of kingship; a new era was initiated with its own calendar; and the assembly of nobles, brahmins, temple dancers, and foreign observers — including the factors of the European trading companies — watched a new sovereign assume the title Chhatrapati. Accounts differ on certain details among the European letters and the Marathi chronicles, but the fact of the coronation itself is unanimous.
significance: The coronation declared, in the most public possible way, that the Maratha country had a rightful sovereign of its own — not a servant of the sultanates or the empire. It completed the transformation begun at Torna: an independent state with a crowned head, its own era, its own law and its own claims to rule. It also institutionalised a new model of legitimacy that resonated for centuries across the subcontinent.

people.name: Shivaji
people.note: Proclaimed Chhatrapati Shiva, 6 June 1674.

people.name: Soyarabai
people.note: Married to Shivaji, with ceremonial roles in the events of the coronation.

people.name: Aurangzeb (counterpart)
people.note: The coronation was a direct assertion against imperial authority.
